newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.African c.bank risking economic overkill - report.
newsitem.headline: S.African c.bank risking economic overkill - report.

text.p: The Reserve Bank has been accused of over-estimating the economy's resilience and urged to stimulate flagging growth by cutting interest rates.

"Investors should be aware of a real danger of the Reserve Bank seriously miscalculating, giving undue weight to misleading money data and being overly protective of the exchange rate," Board of Executors economist Rob Lee said in his latest Investment Outlook on Wednesday.
Lee said the Reserve Bank appeared to be basing its stand on forecasts of a moderate economic slowdown or "soft landing" in 1997, followed by higher growth from next year.
"However, we are coming to believe that an economic overkill, caused by unnecessarily high interest rates, is now a serious possibility," Lee said.
The bank also did not seem to take into account the fact that economic reform had significantly raised South Africa's sustainable growth rate to as much as four percent a year.

It continued to cite the rapid growth in broad money supply (M3) and bank credit as an excuse for not cutting interest rates. This was despite the fact that most central banks had started placing less emphasis on money supply behaviour.
"In South Africa, the process of reintegration into the global economy, on top of other major structural changes, makes it even more likely that money and credit data are misleading," Lee said.
"Relaxation of exchange controls and (central) bank withdrawal from the forward cover market are just two of the many major changes that could distort money data."

The growth in narrow money had been much lower than that of M3 for some time now while credit growth to individuals was lower than to companies, indicating possible structural changes that might not have any inflationary consequences.
At the same time, interest rates remained too high while the 1997/98 budget, if implemented, would result in a "material" slowing down of the economy as government spending fell in real terms.
The Reserve Bank's tough stand on interest rates could be based on scepticism that government would stick to its spending targets, "but what if they are wrong?" Lee asked.
By the end of the year, lower government spending and continued high interest rates would have pushed the economy onto a much lower growth path.
"Reducing interest rates then will do nothing to prevent the economy remaining in the doldrums for another year," Lee said.

Most central banks around the world now operated ahead of forecast trends and did not wait until inflation was rising before raising interest rates. They acted when conditions for higher inflation were developing.

"The little noticed corollary to this is that it should work the other way too - interest rates can begin coming down when it becomes clear that the conditions for lower inflation have developed," Lee said.
He was also critical of the bank's view that interest rates could not be reduced until the impact of the relaxation of exchange controls had been assessed.

The current exchange rate was probably too high and the relaxation of foreign exchange controls would allow for a moderate weakening. At the same time, the inflationary impact of the weak rand had been less than expected because of intense competition and lower import tariffs.
